subject: ela
skillName: Use technology to produce and publish writing
intro: These problems ask you to evaluate digital-writing choices in fuller situations. Each one gives you a multi-sentence scenario, a thread of comments, or a draft excerpt with more than one issue. Weigh how the choices fit the writer's purpose and audience, then explain the single best response.

items.prompt: Maya is finishing a six-page research report on local rivers for her science teacher. She wants the three main sections to stand out, she needs to fix a few typos, and she wants to add a photo of a river with a short label under it. Her teacher will read the report on a school laptop. List the three word-processing features Maya should use, and for each one explain how it serves her stated goal.
items.answer: She should: (1) add headings to label the three main sections so the teacher can find and scan them; (2) run spell check, then reread, to catch the typos a tool may flag and the real-word errors it misses; (3) insert the image and add a caption under it to label the photo. Each feature serves a specific goal rather than just decorating the page.

steps: Identify each stated goal: make three sections stand out, fix typos, add a labeled photo.
Match a feature to the section goal: headings label and separate sections so a reader can scan a long report, which is better than recoloring or italicizing text.
Match a feature to the typo goal: spell check flags many errors, but Maya must still reread because spell check accepts real words used wrongly.
Match a feature to the photo goal: insert the image, then add a caption underneath so the photo is explained, not just placed.
Confirm each choice serves the purpose and audience rather than decorating the page.

items.prompt: Jordan must send a request to the school principal asking permission to start a coding club, and he also wants a few classmates to help him draft the proposal together at the same time before he sends it. For the final request he is choosing between a group text and a formal email; for the drafting he is choosing between everyone editing separate copies and using one shared document. Which tool fits each task, and why?
items.answer: For the final request, a formal email fits best, because it reaches one specific reader directly and supports a respectful, formal tone, while a group text is too casual for a principal. For the drafting, a single shared document fits best, because classmates can write and comment in one place at the same time, instead of merging many separate copies.

steps: Separate the two tasks: a formal request to one adult, and group drafting among peers.
For the request, match tool to audience and purpose: a principal expects a formal, direct message, so a formal email beats a casual group text.
For the drafting, match tool to the need for real-time group work: a shared document lets everyone edit and comment in one place.
Reject separate copies, since merging many versions wastes effort and loses comments.
Confirm each tool fits its purpose and audience.

items.prompt: A student left this comment on a classmate's shared draft about school lunches: 'Your opening grabbed me, but the third paragraph claims that students waste food without any proof. Could you add a number or example from the cafeteria survey?' Explain two things this comment does well and one thing the writer should do in response.
items.answer: The comment does well because it (1) names a specific part, the third paragraph, and the exact problem, a claim with no proof, and (2) stays respectful while suggesting a concrete fix, adding a number or example. In response, the writer should accept the useful feedback and add the requested evidence, replying with a clear next step such as 'Good point, I will add the survey number.'

steps: Check whether the comment is specific: it points to the third paragraph and the unsupported claim, so yes.
Check whether it is respectful and actionable: it opens with genuine praise and suggests a concrete fix, so yes.
Decide the best response to feedback: accept it and state a next step, rather than dismissing or deleting it.
State the improvement the writer should make: add evidence from the survey.
Confirm the response moves the writing forward.

items.prompt: Read this draft excerpt: 'The principle reason our team one the contest was teamwork. There research showed that practice helps.' Spell check flags no errors in these sentences. Find all three real-word errors spell check missed and give the correct word for each.
items.answer: There are three real-word errors: 'principle' should be 'principal' (meaning main); 'one' should be 'won' (the verb); and 'There' should be 'Their' (showing possession). Spell check accepts each because they are all correctly spelled words, just the wrong words for the meaning.

steps: Read for meaning, not just spelling, because spell check cannot catch real words used wrongly.
'principle reason' should be 'principal reason,' since principal means main here.
'team one the contest' should be 'team won the contest,' the verb won.
'There research' should be 'Their research,' showing the research belongs to them.
Confirm all three are correctly spelled words, which is why spell check stayed silent.

items.prompt: On a shared document, three students left comments on Lena's report: Comment 1 says 'I love it, no changes!'; Comment 2 says 'This intro is boring, fix it.'; Comment 3 says 'Your intro states the topic clearly, but it does not tell readers why the topic matters. Adding one sentence on why it matters would pull readers in.' Decide which comment is the most useful for revising the writing, and explain why the other two are less helpful.
items.answer: Comment 3 is the most useful, because it names a specific strength, points to a specific weakness, and suggests a concrete improvement. Comment 1 is vague praise that gives the writer nothing to act on, and Comment 2 is unkind and only labels a problem without saying what to do about it.

steps: Recall that useful feedback is specific, respectful, and actionable.
Comment 1 is only praise, so it gives no direction for revision.
Comment 2 is harsh and vague: it names no fix and uses an unkind tone.
Comment 3 names a strength, a specific weakness, and a concrete fix, so it is the most useful.
Select Comment 3 as the best feedback.

items.prompt: While researching a report, Diego finds a useful paragraph on a website. He is considering four ways to use it: (a) copy the sentences word for word with no mention of the site, (b) change five words and present the idea as his own, (c) put the fact in his own words and name the website as his source, (d) email the fact to a friend. Choose the responsible option and explain why each of the other three is a problem.
items.answer: Option (c) is responsible: putting the fact in his own words and naming the website credits the source and avoids plagiarism. Option (a) is copying without credit, which is plagiarism. Option (b) is also plagiarism, because swapping a few words does not make the idea his own. Option (d) does not help him use the fact responsibly in his report at all.

steps: Recall that responsible use means paraphrasing and crediting the source.
Option (a) copies text with no credit, which is plagiarism.
Option (b) makes small word changes and claims the idea, which is still plagiarism.
Option (d) sends the fact away rather than crediting it in the report.
Option (c) paraphrases and names the source, so it is the responsible choice.

items.prompt: Priya is about to publish her personal essay on the class blog. Her draft ends with: 'You can reach me at 14 Oak Street or call 555-0199, and by the way, Sam's essay was the worst in our class.' Identify the two online-safety and conduct problems in this ending, and rewrite it so it is safe and respectful.
items.answer: Two problems: it shares private personal information (home address and phone number) on a public blog, and it includes an unkind, disrespectful remark about a classmate. A safe, respectful rewrite removes both, for example: 'Thanks for reading. I would love to hear your thoughts in the comments.' This protects personal details and keeps a respectful tone.

steps: Spot the private information: a home address and phone number should never be posted publicly.
Spot the conduct problem: naming a classmate's work as the worst is unkind and disrespectful.
Apply safe-publishing rules: protect personal information and keep a respectful tone.
Rewrite to remove the address, the phone number, and the insult.
Confirm the new ending is both safe and respectful.

items.prompt: Two students replied to the same comment on a shared draft. The comment read: 'Could you add a source for the statistic in paragraph two?' Reply A said: 'Stop telling me what to do, it is fine.' Reply B said: 'Good point, the number came from the city water report. I will add the link in paragraph two.' Decide which reply best moves the writing forward and explain what makes the other reply unhelpful.
items.answer: Reply B best moves the writing forward, because it accepts the useful feedback, identifies the source, and states a clear next step (adding the link). Reply A is defensive and dismissive: it rejects a reasonable request, gives no source, and does not improve the draft.

steps: Identify what the comment asks: provide a source for a statistic.
Reply A reacts defensively and refuses, so the missing source problem stays unfixed.
Reply B accepts the feedback, names the source, and commits to adding the link.
A good response to feedback accepts useful suggestions and states a next step.
Select Reply B as the response that improves the writing.

items.prompt: For a report on healthy eating, Ana is choosing between two websites. Site 1 is a state health department page that lists its authors, gives a recent date, and cites studies. Site 2 is an anonymous post on a snack company's page that has no date and is trying to sell candy. Decide which source is more credible, give two reasons, and describe how Ana should credit it in her report.
items.answer: Site 1 is more credible. Two reasons: it names its authors and shows a recent date, and it cites studies rather than trying to sell a product, while Site 2 is anonymous, undated, and biased toward selling candy. To credit Site 1, Ana should put the facts in her own words and name the state health department as her source.

steps: List signs of credibility: named authors, a recent date, cited studies, and no sales motive.
Site 2 fails these tests: anonymous, undated, and biased toward selling a product.
Site 1 passes these tests, so it is the more credible source.
Decide how to credit it: paraphrase the facts and name the source to avoid plagiarism.
Confirm the choice rests on credibility, not on which site is flashier.

items.prompt: Owen has two hours to type a four-page story in one sitting for a deadline. He usually types with one finger while looking at the keyboard, presses each key very hard, and stops after every word to reread. Explain why each of these three habits will slow him down, and name the keyboarding habit that would best help him finish on time.
items.answer: One-finger typing while watching the keys is slow because his eyes leave the screen and only one finger does the work. Pressing keys very hard tires his hands quickly. Stopping after every word breaks his rhythm and pace. The habit that helps most is resting his fingers on the home row and keeping a steady rhythm, because touch typing builds the speed and stamina to type several pages in one sitting.

steps: Evaluate one-finger, look-at-the-keys typing: it is slow and pulls his eyes off the screen.
Evaluate pressing keys very hard: it tires the hands and reduces stamina.
Evaluate stopping after every word: it breaks rhythm, so overall speed drops.
Identify the better habit: home-row touch typing with a steady rhythm.
Explain why it works: it builds the speed and endurance needed for a multi-page piece in one sitting.

items.prompt: A team is writing a class newsletter that will be emailed to families. Three students each made a different choice. Student 1 colored every word a different color. Student 2 added a clear headline, used bold for each section title, and made one bulleted list of upcoming events. Student 3 set the whole document to italics. Decide whose formatting best serves the families who will read it, and explain why the other two choices hurt readability.
items.answer: Student 2's formatting serves readers best, because a clear headline, bold section titles, and a bulleted list of events help families scan and find information quickly. Student 1's many colors are distracting decoration that does not organize the content, and Student 3's all-italic text is hard to read across a whole document.

steps: Recall the goal: families should be able to read and scan the newsletter easily.
Student 1 uses color as decoration, which distracts rather than organizes.
Student 3 makes everything italic, which is hard to read in long stretches.
Student 2 uses a headline, bold titles, and a bulleted list, which all guide the reader.
Select Student 2's choices as the ones that best serve the audience.

items.prompt: Read this draft excerpt and the situation. The writer typed: 'Are school should aloud longer lunch periods.' Spell check flags nothing. The piece is a formal letter to the school board, but it is written in all lowercase and casual slang. Identify the two real-word errors spell check missed, and name one more change that would make the tone fit the formal audience.
items.answer: The two real-word errors are 'Are' which should be 'Our,' and 'aloud' which should be 'allow' (or 'allow for'). Spell check misses both because they are correctly spelled words. To fit the formal school-board audience, the writer should also use proper capitalization and replace casual slang with formal, respectful wording.

steps: Read for meaning to catch real-word errors spell check accepts.
'Are school' should be 'Our school,' the possessive word.
'should aloud' should be 'should allow,' the verb, not the word meaning out loud.
Match tone to audience: a school board expects formal writing.
Name a tone fix: use correct capitalization and replace casual slang with formal language.

items.prompt: A group is collaborating in one shared document on a report. Three suggested changes appear in the comment column. Comment 1: 'change everything, it is all wrong.' Comment 2: 'In paragraph one, the topic sentence and the first detail say the same thing, so you could cut the repeated detail.' Comment 3: 'add more.' Decide which suggestion the writer should act on first and explain why the other two are hard to use.
items.answer: The writer should act on Comment 2 first, because it points to a specific spot, paragraph one, names a specific problem, repetition, and suggests a concrete fix, cutting the repeated detail. Comment 1 is vague and harsh, giving no direction, and Comment 3 is too vague to act on because it does not say what to add or where.

steps: Recall that an actionable comment names a place, a problem, and a fix.
Comment 1 says everything is wrong but names nothing specific, so it cannot guide a revision.
Comment 3 says 'add more' without saying what or where, so it is too vague.
Comment 2 names paragraph one, the repetition, and the cut to make.
Choose Comment 2 as the suggestion to act on first.

items.prompt: Sara wants to publish a blog post and let readers respond. She is deciding among four plans. Plan A: post it with comments off and include her phone number so readers can text reactions. Plan B: post it, turn on comments, and set a friendly rule asking readers to be respectful and stay on topic. Plan C: post it and reply rudely to anyone who disagrees. Plan D: post a copied article from another site under her own name. Choose the plan that best supports safe, responsible publishing and interaction, and explain why each other plan fails.
items.answer: Plan B is best, because it lets readers interact through comments while keeping a respectful, on-topic space and not sharing private contact details. Plan A exposes her personal phone number, which is unsafe. Plan C uses a rude, disrespectful tone toward readers. Plan D is plagiarism, since it posts someone else's article as her own.

steps: Recall safe, responsible publishing: protect personal information, keep a respectful tone, and credit others' work.
Plan A shares a private phone number publicly, which is unsafe.
Plan C replies rudely, which breaks the respectful-tone rule.
Plan D posts a copied article as her own, which is plagiarism.
Plan B enables interaction while keeping it safe and respectful, so it is the best choice.

items.prompt: Liam's report has several digital-writing problems at once: it has no headings, so the four sections blur together; paragraph three uses a statistic with no source; and it ends by listing his home address. He has time to fix only the issues that matter most for a clear, responsible report his teacher will grade. List the fix for each problem and explain how each one improves the report.
items.answer: Three fixes: (1) add headings to label the four sections so the teacher can scan and find them; (2) credit the source of the statistic in paragraph three, in his own words and naming the source, to avoid plagiarism and support the claim; (3) remove his home address, because private personal information should not be included. Together these make the report clearer, properly sourced, and safe.

steps: Spot the organization issue: no headings, so add headings to label and separate the four sections.
Spot the sourcing issue: a statistic with no source, so paraphrase and name the source to avoid plagiarism.
Spot the safety issue: a home address, so remove the private personal information.
Explain the payoff: clearer structure, a supported and credited claim, and safe content.
Confirm all three fixes serve a clear, responsible report for the teacher.
